demographics: More common with increasing age as cardiopulmonary disease accumulates
Occurs at any age when there is severe lung, neuromuscular or chest wall disease

risk_factors.text: COPD or other chronic obstructive lung disease
Pneumonia or other acute severe lung infection
Congestive heart failure or acute pulmonary edema
Neuromuscular weakness (ALS, muscular dystrophy, spinal cord injury, stroke)
Chest wall deformity or chest trauma
Drug or alcohol overdose with depressed breathing
Smoke inhalation or exposure to harmful fumes
Obesity with obstructive sleep apnea or obesity hypoventilation

social_history: Occupational exposure to dusts or fumes

chief_complaints.text: I feel like I'm not getting enough air
My lips and fingertips look blue
I'm so sleepy I can't stay awake

hpi.onset: Often sudden over minutes to hours when acute; gradual over days to weeks when chronic
hpi.duration: Minutes to hours in acute respiratory failure; weeks to months in chronic respiratory failure
hpi.progression: Breathlessness worsens steadily; confusion, drowsiness or loss of consciousness may develop as oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises
hpi.location: Chest, with a sense of air hunger
hpi.quality: Air hunger and inability to take a satisfying breath
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; can become critical with inability to speak in full sentences

associated_symptoms.text: Bluish color of lips, skin or fingernails
Excessive sleepiness or difficulty staying awake

pertinent_negatives: Sudden sharp chest pain with breathlessness suggesting pulmonary embolism
Fever with productive cough suggesting pneumonia
Crushing chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw suggesting myocardial infarction
Wheezing that improves with an inhaler suggesting simple asthma exacerbation
Recent long bone fracture or immobilization suggesting fat embolism
New focal weakness or slurred speech suggesting stroke

argues_against: Isolated wheeze that resolves with bronchodilator

negatives: Chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, drowsiness or falls rather than breathlessness; bluish discoloration and air hunger may be absent.
Infants and young children show grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions and irritability or lethargy instead of describing breathlessness.
Hypoxemia and rapid breathing may be the only findings; fever and cough are often blunted.
Chronic daytime sleepiness, morning headache and hypoxemia from hypoventilation may dominate without obvious lung disease.

general.mild: Alert, speaking in full sentences, mildly breathless with exertion, no cyanosis
general.moderate: Breathless at rest, speaking in short sentences, using accessory muscles, may be anxious
general.severe: Speaking in words only, sitting upright and tripoding, marked accessory muscle use, dusky or cyanotic lips and fingertips, may be confused or drowsy
general.critical: Exhausted or obtunded, unable to speak, paradoxical breathing or agonal respirations, deeply cyanotic, may be unresponsive

findings.finding: Use of sternocleidomastoid, scalene and intercostal muscles; supraclavicular or intercostal retractions

findings.finding: Sitting upright, leaning forward with arms braced on knees or bed

findings.finding: Bluish discoloration of the lips and oral mucosa

findings.maneuver: Inspect the fingertips and nail beds
findings.finding: Bluish discoloration of the fingertips and nail beds

findings.finding: Speaks in short phrases or single words only

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place and time and level of arousal
findings.finding: Confusion, agitation, drowsiness or reduced level of consciousness

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the skin
findings.finding: Cool, clammy, sweaty skin

findings.maneuver: Observe the nares during breathing
findings.finding: Flaring of the nostrils with each breath

findings.maneuver: Auscultate over the lung fields and time the expiratory phase

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the posterior and anterior lung fields with the diaphragm of the stethoscope

findings.maneuver: Auscultate and compare breath sounds in all lung fields

findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to extend both arms with wrists dorsiflexed and observe for 30 seconds
findings.finding: Flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, suggesting carbon dioxide retention

findings.maneuver: Test strength, sensation and cranial nerves briefly
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss or cranial nerve deficit

findings.maneuver: Measure the temperature and review the trend
findings.finding: No fever

labs.caveat: Measured on room air when possible; a PaO2 under 60 mm Hg on room air defines hypoxemic respiratory failure.
A PaCO2 over 45 mm Hg with respiratory acidosis defines hypercapnic respiratory failure; a normal or low PaCO2 does not exclude it in chronic compensation.
Acidemia indicates acute or acute-on-chronic failure; a near-normal pH with high PaCO2 suggests chronic compensated retention.
A negative base excess reflects a metabolic component, often lactic acidosis from hypoperfusion.
Elevated bicarbonate indicates chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation; a low value suggests a coexisting metabolic acidosis.
Elevated lactate suggests tissue hypoperfusion or anaerobic metabolism and marks a sicker patient.
Leukocytosis supports infection as the cause; leukopenia can occur in severe sepsis and is a poor prognostic sign.
Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and worsens tissue hypoxia.
Elevated BNP supports heart failure or fluid overload as the cause of respiratory failure.
Elevated troponin suggests myocardial injury, demand ischemia or acute coronary syndrome as a contributor.
Rising creatinine suggests hypoperfusion, dehydration or a cardiorenal process.
Hyperkalemia can accompany acidosis and renal failure and increases arrhythmia risk.
Supports bacterial infection as the cause and can guide antibiotic decisions.
Elevated in pulmonary embolism but nonspecific; use with pretest probability, not as a stand-alone rule-out in a hypoxemic inpatient.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation or other atrial arrhythmia
Tachycardia
Premature ventricular complexes or ventricular arrhythmia
ST depression or T-wave inversion suggesting demand ischemia or myocardial injury
Nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay or bundle branch block
Signs of right heart strain (S1Q3T3, right axis deviation, T-wave inversion in V1–V3) suggesting pulmonary embolism

imaging.preferred_when: First-line in almost every patient with suspected respiratory failure

findings.text: Bilateral alveolar or interstitial opacities suggesting pulmonary edema or pneumonia
Focal consolidation suggesting pneumonia
Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms and increased retrosternal air space suggesting COPD
Enlarged cardiac silhouette and pleural effusions suggesting heart failure
Normal chest x-ray (for example in pulmonary embolism, neuromuscular weakness or early ARDS)
Pneumothorax with visible pleural line and absent lung markings
Diffuse bilateral opacities without cardiomegaly suggesting ARDS

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism when pretest probability is not low

findings.text: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries confirming pulmonary embolism
Right ventricular enlargement suggesting right heart strain
Pulmonary infarction with peripheral wedge-shaped opacity

imaging.preferred_when: Unclear cause after chest x-ray, or suspected parenchymal or pleural disease

findings.text: Consolidation, ground-glass opacities or tree-in-bud nodularity suggesting infection
Bilateral dependent ground-glass and consolidation suggesting ARDS
Pleural effusion or empyema
Interstitial fibrosis or emphysema suggesting chronic lung disease

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected stroke or depressed consciousness of unclear cause

findings.text: Acute infarct or hemorrhage explaining central hypoventilation or aspiration
No acute intracranial abnormality

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the chest and pleural space
imaging.preferred_when: Bedside assessment of pleural effusion, consolidation or pneumothorax

findings.text: Pleural effusion with anechoic fluid and lung compression
Consolidated lung with hepatization and air bronchograms
Absent lung sliding suggesting pneumothorax

imaging.preferred_when: Pulmonary embolism suspected when CT contrast is contraindicated (renal failure, severe contrast allergy, pregnancy)

findings.text: Mismatched segmental perfusion defect with normal ventilation suggesting pulmonary embolism
Normal or low-probability study

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected cardiogenic cause or hemodynamic instability

findings.text: Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction with regional or global wall motion abnormality
Left atrial enlargement, diastolic dysfunction or valvular disease
Right ventricular dilation and dysfunction suggesting acute pulmonary embolism or cor pulmonale
Pericardial effusion with or without tamponade physiology

initial.why: Looks for stroke or intracranial cause of hypoventilation

Not part of the routine respiratory failure workup

decision_points: Arterial blood gas on room air when possible to classify hypoxemic versus hypercapnic failure and assess acid-base status
Chest x-ray first in almost every patient; CT pulmonary angiography if pulmonary embolism is suspected and pretest probability is not low
Do not delay oxygen and ventilatory support for diagnostic testing in a patient with severe hypoxemia or altered mental status
Consider noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD exacerbation or pulmonary edema; intubate if it fails or the patient cannot protect the airway
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Respiratory failure (arterial blood gas definition)
criteria.summary: Respiratory failure is present when the arterial blood gas shows a PaO2 below 60 mm Hg on room air (hypoxemic) or a PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg with respiratory acidosis (hypercapnic); both may coexist.
items: PaO2 under 60 mm Hg on room air
PaCO2 over 45 mm Hg with pH under 7.35

differential.name: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea, hypoxemia, crackles and orthopnea are shared with respiratory failure from any cause; cardiogenic pulmonary edema is one of the most common causes of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, an S3 gallop, or bilateral basal crackles with a third heart sound

history: Progressive orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Known heart failure, coronary disease or valvular disease
Leg swelling and rapid weight gain
Improves with sitting upright and diuresis
labs: Elevated troponin suggesting demand ischemia or acute coronary syndrome
Normal or mildly elevated white count
imaging: Chest x-ray with cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular congestion, Kerley B lines and pleural effusions
Echocardiogram showing reduced ejection fraction or diastolic dysfunction

differential.name: Pneumonia with sepsis
differential.why_considered: Fever, productive cough, hypoxemia and tachypnea are shared; severe pneumonia is a leading cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
differential.trigger: Fever with productive cough, focal crackles, and leukocytosis or leukopenia

history: Fever and chills
Productive cough with purulent sputum
Pleuritic chest pain
Recent upper respiratory infection or aspiration event
exam: Focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds
Dullness to percussion over the affected lobe
imaging: Focal lobar or segmental consolidation on chest x-ray
CT showing consolidation, air bronchograms or tree-in-bud nodularity

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia and tachypnea without obvious lung disease; a classic must-not-miss cause of acute respiratory failure.
differential.trigger: Sudden dyspnea with clear lungs, pleuritic chest pain, or risk factors such as immobility, recent surgery or active cancer

history: Sudden onset of dyspnea
Pleuritic chest pain or hemoptysis
Recent surgery, immobility, long travel or active cancer
Prior venous thromboembolism
exam: Tachycardia and tachypnea with clear lungs
Signs of deep vein thrombosis (unilateral leg swelling and tenderness)
Hypotension or syncope in massive embolism
labs: Elevated troponin or BNP suggesting right heart strain
imaging: Filling defect in pulmonary arteries on CT pulmonary angiography
Right ventricular enlargement on CT or echocardiogram
Mismatched segmental perfusion defect on V/Q scan when CT contrast is contraindicated
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern, right axis deviation, or T-wave inversion in V1–V3 suggesting right heart strain

differential.name: COPD exacerbation
differential.why_considered: Worsening dyspnea, wheezing and hypercapnia are shared; COPD exacerbation is a common cause of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

history: Known COPD with chronic productive cough and exercise limitation
Gradual worsening over days
Increased sputum volume or purulence
Long smoking history
exam: Barrel chest and diminished breath sounds
labs: Elevated bicarbonate suggesting chronic CO2 retention
imaging: Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms and increased retrosternal air space on chest x-ray

differential.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
differential.why_considered: Severe hypoxemia with diffuse bilateral opacities and no cardiogenic cause; ARDS is a common final pathway of many causes of respiratory failure.

history: Recent sepsis, aspiration, severe pneumonia, pancreatitis or major trauma
Rapid onset within one week of the inciting event
exam: Severe hypoxemia out of proportion to exam findings
labs: PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300 despite high oxygen
No evidence of elevated left atrial pressure
imaging: Bilateral diffuse alveolar and interstitial opacities without cardiomegaly or pleural effusion
CT showing dependent ground-glass and consolidation

differential.name: Neuromuscular respiratory failure
differential.why_considered: Hypoventilation with hypercapnia and preserved lung parenchyma; causes include ALS, muscular dystrophy, spinal cord injury and stroke.

history: Progressive limb weakness, difficulty swallowing or slurred speech
Known neuromuscular disease
Recent spinal cord injury or stroke
labs: Hypercapnia with a relatively normal PaO2 early
imaging: Normal chest x-ray or only basal atelectasis
CT head showing infarct or hemorrhage when central cause is suspected

differential.name: Opioid or sedative overdose with hypoventilation
differential.why_considered: Depressed respiratory drive causing hypercapnia and hypoxemia; a reversible and time-critical cause of respiratory failure.
differential.trigger: Pinpoint pupils, depressed consciousness and slow shallow breathing in a patient with access to opioids or sedatives

history: Known opioid or benzodiazepine use
Recent dose escalation or intentional overdose
Bystanders report the patient was difficult to wake
labs: Toxicology screen positive for opioids or sedatives
imaging: No acute intracranial abnormality on CT head

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea and hypoxemia with unilateral absent breath sounds; tension pneumothorax is immediately life-threatening.
differential.trigger: Sudden dyspnea with unilateral absent breath sounds, hyperresonance and hemodynamic instability

history: Sudden sharp chest pain and dyspnea
Recent chest trauma, central line placement or mechanical ventilation
Known lung disease such as COPD or Marfan syndrome
exam: Absent breath sounds on one side
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side in tension pneumothorax
Hypotension and distended neck veins in tension pneumothorax
imaging: Visible pleural line with absent lung markings on chest x-ray
Absent lung sliding on bedside ultrasound
Deep sulcus sign on supine film

severity.mild: Mild hypoxemia (SpO2 90–94% or PaO2 60–79 mm Hg) with normal or near-normal pH, alert patient speaking in full sentences, no accessory muscle use, responds to low-flow oxygen
severity.moderate: Moderate hypoxemia (SpO2 85–90% or PaO2 50–60 mm Hg) with mild respiratory acidosis, breathless at rest, using accessory muscles, may need noninvasive ventilation or higher-flow oxygen
severity.severe: Severe hypoxemia (SpO2 75–85% or PaO2 40–50 mm Hg) with significant hypercapnia and acidemia, speaking in words only, tripoding, cyanosis, confusion or drowsiness, often needs intubation and mechanical ventilation
severity.critical: Life-threatening failure with SpO2 below 75% or PaO2 below 40 mm Hg, severe acidemia (pH below 7.1), exhaustion, obtundation, paradoxical or agonal respirations, or hemodynamic collapse; immediate intubation and ICU care

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status, confusion or drowsiness
red_flags.meaning: Cerebral hypoxemia or CO2 narcosis; indicates severe respiratory failure and impending respiratory arrest

red_flags.finding: Inability to speak in full sentences or single-word speech
red_flags.meaning: Severe respiratory distress with limited reserve; prepare for ventilatory support

red_flags.finding: Central cyanosis of lips or oral mucosa
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; immediate oxygen and escalation of support

red_flags.finding: Exhaustion, paradoxical abdominal movement or agonal respirations
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory arrest; intubate without delay
Shock or severe acidosis; consider sepsis, tension pneumothorax or massive pulmonary embolism

red_flags.finding: Silent chest in a previously wheezing patient
red_flags.meaning: Airflow too low to generate sound; imminent respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Unilateral absent breath sounds with tracheal deviation
red_flags.meaning: Tension pneumothorax; needle decompression before imaging

red_flags.finding: Pinpoint pupils with depressed consciousness and slow breathing
red_flags.meaning: Opioid toxicity; give naloxone and support ventilation

complications.name: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
clues: Persistent altered mental status after oxygenation improves

complications.name: Ventilator-associated pneumonia
clues: New fever and purulent secretions after 48 hours of mechanical ventilation

complications.name: Barotrauma and pneumothorax
clues: Sudden deterioration on positive pressure ventilation

complications.name: Critical illness myopathy and neuropathy
clues: Diffuse weakness after sedation is stopped

complications.name: Post-intensive care syndrome
clues: Cognitive impairment, anxiety, depression or post-traumatic stress after ICU discharge
Persistent weakness and reduced exercise tolerance

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, drowsiness or falls rather than breathlessness; bluish discoloration and air hunger may be absent, so pulse oximetry and blood gas are essential.
Infants and young children show grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions and irritability or lethargy instead of describing breathlessness; respiratory rate norms are age-dependent.

Physiologic changes reduce functional residual capacity and increase oxygen consumption, so hypoxemia develops faster; left lateral tilt improves venous return; pregnancy test before CT and consider V/Q scan if CT contrast is contraindicated.
Hypoxemia and rapid breathing may be the only findings; fever and cough are often blunted, and opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia should be considered.
Chronic daytime sleepiness, morning headache and hypoxemia from hypoventilation may dominate without obvious lung disease; noninvasive ventilation is often effective.
Avoid iodinated contrast for CT pulmonary angiography when possible; use V/Q scan instead; watch for hyperkalemia and acidosis worsening respiratory drive.

key_questions.question: When did the breathing trouble start, and how fast has it gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over minutes to hours suggests pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema or opioid overdose; gradual worsening over days suggests pneumonia, COPD exacerbation or neuromuscular weakness

key_questions.question: Can you say a whole sentence, or do you have to stop for breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Speaking in short phrases or single words marks severe distress and limited respiratory reserve

key_questions.question: Does it get worse when you lie flat, and do you wake up at night short of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to cardiogenic pulmonary edema

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough, and are you bringing anything up? What color is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Purulent or blood-tinged sputum suggests pneumonia; hemoptysis raises pulmonary embolism

key_questions.question: Have you had any chest pain, and is it sharp or does it hurt more when you breathe in?
key_questions.looking_for: Pleuritic pain suggests pulmonary embolism, pneumonia or pneumothorax; pressure-like pain suggests cardiac ischemia

key_questions.question: Have you felt confused, unusually sleepy, or had trouble staying awake?
key_questions.looking_for: Confusion or drowsiness from hypoxemia or CO2 retention indicates severe respiratory failure and impending arrest

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and chills suggest pneumonia or sepsis as the cause

key_questions.question: Do you have any known lung or heart problems, like COPD, asthma or heart failure?
key_questions.looking_for: Known COPD or heart failure makes exacerbation or decompensation the likely cause

key_questions.question: Have you had any weakness, trouble swallowing, slurred speech or a recent stroke or spinal injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Neuromuscular disease or central injury causing hypoventilation with clear lungs

key_questions.question: What medicines do you take, especially pain pills, sleeping pills or anything for anxiety?
key_questions.looking_for: Opioids, benzodiazepines or other sedatives can depress respiratory drive and cause hypercapnic failure

key_questions.question: Have you been around smoke, fumes or chemicals, or had a recent injury to your chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoke inhalation, toxic fumes or chest trauma causing respiratory failure

key_questions.question: Have you been immobile, had recent surgery, a long trip or been treated for a blood clot before?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for pulmonary embolism as the cause of sudden hypoxemia

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and for how many years?
key_questions.looking_for: Long smoking history supports COPD as the underlying cause

key_questions.question: Have you had any swelling in your legs or sudden weight gain?
key_questions.looking_for: Peripheral edema and rapid weight gain suggest heart failure or fluid overload

reasoning_points: Recognizes that respiratory failure is defined by arterial blood gas, not by symptoms alone: PaO2 below 60 mm Hg on room air (hypoxemic) or PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg with respiratory acidosis (hypercapnic), and that both can coexist
Classifies the failure as hypoxemic, hypercapnic or mixed and notes whether it is acute, chronic or acute-on-chronic using pH and bicarbonate
Identifies the underlying cause from history, exam and initial tests rather than treating the number alone

Names the common causes to consider: COPD exacerbation, pneumonia, heart failure with pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, ARDS, neuromuscular weakness, opioid or sedative overdose and chest wall problems
Uses pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas to quantify severity and guide oxygen and ventilatory support
Orders a chest x-ray first in almost every patient and escalates to CT pulmonary angiography or CT chest when the cause remains unclear
Recognizes red flags for impending respiratory arrest: altered mental status, single-word speech, central cyanosis, exhaustion, paradoxical breathing and silent chest
Does not delay oxygen and ventilatory support for diagnostic testing in a severely hypoxemic or obtunded patient
Considers noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic failure from COPD exacerbation or pulmonary edema and knows when to intubate
Reviews medications for opioids, benzodiazepines and other sedatives that depress respiratory drive
Considers pregnancy before CT imaging and chooses V/Q scan when CT contrast is contraindicated

easy: Older adult with known COPD presenting with worsening dyspnea, wheezing and prolonged expiration
Arterial blood gas shows hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis and elevated bicarbonate
Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms
Responds to bronchodilators and noninvasive ventilation
medium: Patient with fever, productive cough and focal crackles; blood gas shows hypoxemia and chest x-ray shows lobar consolidation
Patient with orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure and an S3 gallop; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary vascular congestion
Sudden dyspnea with clear lungs and tachycardia after recent surgery or immobility, raising pulmonary embolism
Older adult presenting with confusion and drowsiness rather than breathlessness
hard: Neuromuscular weakness with hypercapnia and a normal chest x-ray, where the lungs themselves are not the problem
Opioid or sedative overdose with pinpoint pupils, depressed consciousness and slow shallow breathing
Tension pneumothorax with unilateral absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation and hypotension requiring decompression before imaging
ARDS with severe hypoxemia and diffuse bilateral opacities without cardiomegaly, where the trigger is sepsis or aspiration
Pregnant patient with hypoxemia where imaging must be chosen carefully and hypoxemia develops faster
Immunocompromised patient with hypoxemia but blunted fever and cough, suggesting an opportunistic infection
